328.definition: The elliptical part of the note. Can be either filled in (black) or outlined (white).

329.definition: A vertical line that originates at the notehead, used to indicate rhythm and voicing.

330.definition: The horizontal lines that connect certain groups of notes together.

332.definition: A curved line placed at the end of a stem. Each flag added to a stemmed note represents the reduction of the note value by half. For example, the symbol for an eighth note is like a quarter note plus a flag; the eighth note is one-half the value of the quarter note.

504.definition: Related to European or American culture.

876.definition: A large-scale song structure, in which the same basic multi-phrase unit is repeated throughout (AAA). The basic unit that is repeated is called a strophe. Strophic form is more common in early rock-and-roll (1950s–1960s) than in the 1970s and beyond.

877.definition: A basic multi-phrase unit. In pop music, a strophe is a focal module within strophic-form and AABA-form songs.

929.definition: A musical sound that has both a pitch and a rhythmic component; the symbol may include a stem, beam, and/or flag.

931.definition: The duration of musical sounds and rests in time.

951.definition: Five evenly spaced horizontal lines on which notes are placed.

956.definition: A symbol placed on the left side of a staff that indicates which notes are assigned to different lines and spaces.

966.definition: As a "G" clef, the treble clef designates the second-lowest line of a staff as G₄ by curling around it.

967.definition: As an "F" clef, the bass clef shows which line of the staff is F₃ by surrounding it with two dots.

968.definition: As a "C" clef, the alto clef shows that C₄ is the middle line of the staff by centering on it.

969.definition: As a "C" clef, the tenor clef shows that the second-highest line of the staff is C₄ by centering on that line.

970.definition: A prototypical chord progression or formal structure.

971.definition: Typically comprises three phrases of four bars each. The first phrase is entirely tonic harmony (I). The second phrase contains two bars of subdominant (IV) and two bars of tonic (I). The final phrase begins with one bar of dominant (V) followed by one bar of subdominant (IV) and two bars of tonic (I). The third phrase may or may not end with a turnaround.

973.definition: A variation on the 12-bar blues progression. Typically composed of four four-bar phrases, usually two iterations of tonic, followed by subdominant and dominant. The final phrase may or may not end with a turnaround.

974.definition: The use of a non-tonic chord (usually dominant) at the end of a harmonically closed unit to transition into the beginning of the following on-tonic unit. In jazz, the term "turnaround" often refers to the progression vi–ii–V–I. The exact qualities of these chords are highly variable, and one or more of the chords may be substituted with a different, related chord.

975.definition: A repeated bass pattern that forms the foundation for a set of variations, not unlike the cyclical progressions of pop/rock songs.

979.definition: The highest-level division of the overall form of the piece. Examples include the exposition in sonata form, the first part of a binary form, or the chorus of a pop song.

984.definition: A poetic foot consisting of two stressed syllables in a row.

987.definition: A module or phrase is lyric-variant if each time it appears it brings (mostly) different lyrics.

988.definition: A module or phrase is lyric-invariant if each time it appears it brings (mostly) the same lyrics. Lyric invariance tends to come at points of formal closure (tail refrains at the ends of strophes, choruses at the end of a verse-chorus song’s formal cycle).

989.definition: A module or phrase is music-variant if each time it appears it brings (mostly) different music.

991.definition: A module or phrase is music-invariant if each time it appears it brings (mostly) the same music.

994.definition: A process where modules are stripped away from the formal cycle until only the chorus module (C) remains.

996.definition: A phrase or module is on-tonic when it begins with tonic harmony (I in root position).

997.definition: A phrase or module is off-tonic when it begins on a harmony other than tonic.

998.definition: A phrase or module is harmonically closed when it ends with tonic harmony (I in root position).

999.definition: A phrase or module is harmonically open when it ends on a harmony other than tonic.

1000.definition: Closing rhetoric involves common patterns and techniques that signal that the end of the song is likely coming soon.

1008.definition: Also called 32-bar song form. AABA consists of at least four sections. It begins by repeating two strophes, moving to a contrasting bridge section, and then repeating the primary strophe again. AABA forms typically then include another repetition of BA, making the entire form AABABA.

1012.definition: A type of contrasting section that tends to function transitionally in the formal cycle. Bridges tend to emphasize non-tonic harmonies and commonly end on dominant harmony.

1013.definition: The most common form of pop songs today, consisting of lyric-variant verses and lyric- and music-invariant choruses that deliver the primary narrative material of the song.

1014.definition: Introduction sections transition from the unmetered silence that precedes the song to the musical activity of the first core section. They tend to be short and untexted (i.e., instrumental) and tend to present musical material from one or more core sections to come.

1016.definition: Mid-song intros function similarly to introductions, but in the middle of the song. They usually introduce the first section in the formal cycle.

1017.definition: Outros function as a transition from song back to silence, and thus decrease energy. Often this is accomplished in the recording studio by way of a fadeout.

1018.definition: A coda is a song-ending section that presents new material. Like outros, codas exhibit closing rhetoric.

1019.definition: A lyric-invariant passage within a section that is otherwise lyric-variant. A refrain is too short to form its own section—typically a phrase or less.

1020.definition: A refrain that is the last line or so of a section's text.

1021.definition: A refrain that is the first line or so of the section's text.

1087.definition: Small lines written above or below a staff to extend the staff's range of notes.

1208.definition: Refers to the various ways in which a phrase may be constructed of subphrases, ideas, and motives. Examples of phrase-level forms include sentences, periods, repeated phrases, and hybrid forms.

1209.definition: A unit in some phrase-level forms that is one level smaller than a phrase, but one level larger than an idea.

1210.definition: The smallest unit of music identified by a segmentation analysis. Ideas need not end with cadences, and they may combine to form subphrases or phrases. Examples include basic idea, contrasting idea, unit, cadential idea, and fragments.

1211.definition: A regularly recurring unit of music that's smaller than an idea, and which is typically transformed across a work. The word "motive" usually refers to pitch material, but other kinds of motives such as rhythmic or contour also exist.

1212.definition: Making the durations of a motive last longer than the original.

1213.definition: Making the durations of a motive shorter than the original.

1215.definition: Changing the metric position of the motive relative to its original statement.

1220.definition: A relatively complete musical thought that exhibits trajectory toward a goal (often a cadence).

1221.definition: The way a passage might be shaped in performance (where to push and pull the tempo, where and how to change dynamic levels, etc.).

1222.definition: The process of dividing a passage or piece of music into its component parts.

1223.definition: A melodic and harmonic goal. In classical tonal music, cadence types include Perfect Authentic (PAC), Imperfect Authentic (IAC), and Half (HC).

1225.definition: Refers to the structure of a passage or piece. Form can be understood as a hierarchical grouping of units, and we often speak of form at one of two levels: phrase-level form (referring to motives, ideas, subphrases, or phrases) or composition-level form (referring to sections, movements, or whole pieces).

1263.definition: A technique used to aid memorization.

1288.definition: The span of notes a voice or instrument can produce.

1327.definition: Relating to movement of parts of the body.

1329.definition: To imagine hearing a sound in one's mind.

1344.definition: Two staves placed one above the other, connected by a brace. The top staff has a treble clef, while the bottom staff has a bass clef.

1363.definition: C₄; the C near the middle of the piano keyboard, written on the first ledger line below the treble clef staff or the first ledger line above the bass clef staff.

1462.definition: The role that a musical element plays in the creation of a larger musical unit.

1465.definition: The norms or principles according to which musical elements are combined into meaningful and stylistically appropriate successions.

1467.definition: Auxiliary sections help frame the core sections: introducing them, providing temporary relief from them, or winding down from them.

1468.definition: Core sections comprise the main musical and poetic content of a song. Core sections include strophe (AABA and strophic form only), bridge, verse, chorus, prechorus, and postchorus.

1475.definition: A symbol that alters a pitch, such as the sharp (♯), flat (♭), and natural (♮) symbols.

1477.definition: Raises a note by a half step.

1479.definition: Lowers a note by a half step.

1488.definition: A core section of a popular song that is lyric-invariant and contains the primary lyrical material of the song. Chorus function is also typified by heightened musical intensity relative to the verse. Chorus sections are distinct from refrains, which are contained within a section.

1489.definition: Sections that are lyric-variant and often contain lyrics that advance the narrative.

1499.definition: One-twelfth of an octave; generally considered to be the smallest interval in Western musical notation.

1504.definition: An interval equal to two half steps

1517.definition: Prechorus function is most significantly typified in energy gain. Prechorus sections often use motivic fragmentation, acceleration of harmonic rhythm, movement away from tonic harmony, and harmonic openness.

1518.definition: A short section that follows a chorus and serves only to close the cycle—does not introduce or transition to the beginning of the next cycle.

1519.definition: A grouping that contains one or more sections, typically in the same order. Sometimes one or more sections are omitted in the repetition of a cycle, especially toward the end of a song.

1550.definition: Raises a note by two half steps.

1552.definition: Lowers a note by two half steps.

1567.definition: A quality in a passage of music that heightens the perceived energy of the passage. This can be through more active rhythmic activity, faster harmony changes, thicker texture, expanded range, crescendo, or drive toward a cadence or goal.

1651.definition: A relationship between notes, intervals, or chords that sound the same but are spelled differently.

1709.definition:
𝄆I – VI – IV – V 𝄇, or C – Ami – F – G in C major.

Common alterations: substituting ii for IV; rotation.

1769.definition: I–V–vi–IV in major, or III–VII–i–VI in minor (C–G–Ami–F, for example). This chord progression often loops throughout a pop song. Frequently, this progression begins on the vi/i chord instead of the I/III chord.

1770.definition: A property of certain chord progressions, where the progression does not inherently imply a single chord as the tonic chord.

1797.definition: IV–V–vi–I. This four-chord schema has become increasingly common in pop music since 2010.

1826.definition: A special kind of phrase consisting of a presentation and a continuation.

1827.definition: Basic ideas are short units that are typically associated with beginnings. They don't usually end with cadences, and they often establish tonic. They are the first units we hear in a presentation, an antecedent, a consequent, and a compound basic idea.

1831.definition: A subphrase consisting of a basic idea and its repetition. Presentations don't usually end with cadences.

1832.definition: A subphrase that features a mix of any of the following: fragmentation, increase in harmonic rhythm, increase in surface rhythm, or sequences. Continuations end with a cadence and are usually found in the second half of a theme.

1844.definition: Making unit sizes smaller than the previously established size. For example, if units had previously been two measures long, fragments might be one measure long.

1845.definition: A pattern that is repeated and transposed by some consistent interval. A sequence may occur in the melody, the harmony, or both.

1846.definition: The rate at which chords change, usually expressed in chords per measure. A common rate of chord change in 18th-century classical music is one chord per measure, for example.

1847.definition: A segment of music that expresses whatever the prevailing higher-level grouping expresses. For example, if a unit is contained within a continuation, it expresses continuation function. We often apply the term "unit" to ideas that aren't easily categorized using terms such as basic idea, contrasting idea, or cadential idea.

1852.definition: A phrase-level form that consists of two phrases: an antecedent and a consequent.

1853.definition: A phrase consisting of a basic idea followed by a contrasting idea that ends with a weak cadence.

1854.definition: A small unit that contrasts with the material that came immediately before it, usually in terms of contour. It's featured in the antecedent and the compound basic idea.

1855.definition: A phrase consisting of a basic idea followed by a contrasting idea that ends with a strong cadence. It usually forms the second half of a phrase-level form.

1859.definition: Two phrases where the second one is a repetition of the first. The repetition is always written out (repeat signs don't signify a repeated phrase), and usually the repetition is a variation on the initial statement.

1862.definition: Occurs when one form is composed of other smaller forms. For example, a period may be composed of two sentences, or one or more of a ternary form's sections may be composed of a binary form.

1870.definition: Replacing a standard chord (i.e., within a harmonic schema) with a different chord. The substituted chord is typically identical in harmonic function to the standard chord, and often shares at least two notes with the standard chord.

1872.definition: Beginning a harmonic schema on a different chord within the schema, but proceeding through the harmonies in the same order.

1882.definition: A 7̂ that is one half step below 1̂. The leading tone is diatonic in major keys, but requires an accidental in minor keys.

1883.definition: The distance between roots of adjacent chords. For example, "root motion by step" refers to the distance between two chords that are only one step apart, such as I and ii, IV and V, etc. Note that the root is not always in the bass, so this is a separate concept from bass motion.

1897.definition: A cadence with the harmonies V–I. The harmonies are typically in root position. Authentic cadences can be further distinguished by their melody note in the I chord: an authentic cadence ending on 1̂ in the melody is a perfect authentic cadence, while one with 3̂ or 5̂ in the melody is an imperfect authentic cadence.

1898.definition: A plagal cadence uses the harmonies IV–I.

1925.definition: A perceived quality created in music through tonic expansions, regular hypermeter, absence of modulations, diatonic melodies, and diatonic harmonies, among other things.

1928.definition: The lengthening of a phrase, whether internally or externally, beyond its expected duration.

1930.definition: A term used to describe a piece's overall tonic. If a movement is in the key of A major, then the home key is A major. The term is used to distinguish itself from local keys.

1932.definition: A symbol (′) that is used in the analysis of phrases and forms to indicate that some repeated material has changed, in some way, from its initial statement.

1938.definition: A piece that has one overarching tonic, that is, it starts and ends in the same key and contains a single tonic that gives the impression of being the primary key of the work.

1941.definition: A piece that starts and ends with different tonics. Compare with monotonality, which is the default harmonic plan in most tonal works from the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries.

2003.definition: Harmony that is based in a diatonic scale, such as the white notes of the piano. In analysis, diatonic harmonies may be labeled with with Roman numerals.

2004.definition: A category of chords that sound stable, providing a sense of home or center. The I chord is the paradigmatic tonic-function chord, but vi and iii occasionally have tonic function.

2005.definition: A harmonic function that may either lead toward a dominant-function chord or back to a tonic-function chord. Subdominant function is most typically associated with the [strong]IV chord[/strong], otherwise known as the subdominant chord, and the [strong]II chord[/strong], otherwise known as the supertonic chord.

2006.definition: A category of chords that provides a sense of urgency to resolve toward the tonic chord, including V and vii° (in minor: V and vii°).

2012.definition: A group of pitches being used as the basis for a composition. This term is more neutral than "key," which may imply a hierarchy.

2017.definition: A section of a work that bears repeat signs, like either of the parts of a binary form.

2019.definition: A type of binary form where the material at the start of reprise 1 returns somewhere near the middle of reprise 2. Both appearances of that repeated music are expected to be in the home key.

2022.definition: A binary form (either simple or rounded) in which the tail end of the first reprise returns at the tail end of the second reprise.

2024.definition: A type of binary form that does not contain the thematic return of a rounded binary. Instead, the second reprise continues with A material without ever having departed from it (thus there is no “return”), or it contains relatively new material throughout.

2028.definition: A type of ternary form where at least one of the form's parts (A, B, or the second A section) is composed of its own complete form (typically a binary form). The term "compound" can also be used to clarify that a single section contains a complete form. Compare with simple ternary form.

2047.definition: An attribute of a musical form where no sections of music return. Similar motivic material may be present in different sections, but the sections would each be considered distinct.

2084.definition: Chromatically altered from the typical version.

2085.definition: For modes in pop music, the color note is the pitch that distinguishes a mode from major (in the case of mixolydian/lydian) or from minor (in the case of dorian/phrygian).

2087.definition: ♭VII–IV–I, or B♭–F–C in C major. The term comes from duplicating the plagal relationship (IV–I) by applying it to IV as well (IV/IV–IV, or ♭VII–IV).

2107.definition: Phrases that are "archetypal" or that follow an archetype are related to the sentence, the period, or one of the hybrid phrase-level forms.

2108.definition: A phrase form that combines aspects of the sentence and the period into one phrase-level form.

2110.definition: The contrasting beginning is like an antecedent without a cadence. It is a beginning part of a phrase-level form that consists of a basic idea followed by a contrasting idea, and it doesn't end with a cadence.

2118.definition: A subphrase that harmonizes the core bass pattern mi–fa–sol–do (3̂–4̂–5̂–1̂). Functions similarly to a continuation.

2121.definition: The process by which a non-tonic triad is made to sound like a temporary tonic. It involves the use of secondary dominant or leading-tone chords.

2150.definition: A term used when describing the sections of a rondo form that are not the main theme (a.k.a. A or refrain). Episodes provide contrast with the main theme through changes in multiple domains, primarily key and melodic/rhythmic/harmonic material.

2155.definition: The primary theme of a rondo-form work, typically stated at the beginning, after each contrasting episode, and as the last section (though a coda may follow).

2161.definition: A perceived characteristic of music that is created by conventional theme types, harmonic stability, symmetrical groupings, and consistent motivic material.

2164.definition: A perceived characteristic of music that is created by unconventional phrase structures, unstable harmonies, diverse motivic material, and so on. Loose organization is common in passages with transitional function.

2221.definition: The tonic chord is present, but weakened. Usually, the weakening comes from using the tonic chord in inversion, or otherwise from placing the tonic chord in a metrically unstable mid-phrase position (versus a more typical usage where the tonic is a stable point of arrival or departure).

2223.definition: A tonic that is initially absent for the first sections of a song, but arrives later on (often in the chorus). Often tied to lyrical themes of attained triumph, self-confidence, or clarity.

2245.definition: A call-and-response texture in which musical material is passed from group to group.

2273.definition: A compound basic idea (c.b.i.) is an antecedent without a cadence. It consists of a basic idea followed by a contrasting idea.

2279.definition: A core bass pattern is the basic series of notes that defines a common progression. This series of notes may be embellished with other, less important notes, but the pattern is still recognizable because the basic series is still present.

2284.definition: One of the three common ending types. Its distinguishing characteristic is its bass line: mi–fa–sol–do (3̂–4̂–5̂–1̂), which may be elaborated with chromaticism.

2295.definition: The process of making a phrase longer than expected. This lengthening might occur within the phrase (internal expansion) or outside of the phrase (external expansion).

2296.definition: Contraction refers to the process of making a phrase shorter than expected. It always occurs within a phrase.

2297.definition: A technique of internal phrase expansion. Sometimes a composer repeats material to create extra length in a phrase. Such repetitions may be exact or varied.

2298.definition: A technique of internal phrase expansion. It occurs when a composer lengthens a harmony or melody by increasing its duration so that it lasts longer than expected. When that happens, we say that the unit that contains the harmony or melody has been stretched.

2299.definition: A technique of internal phrase expansion. Coined by Janet Schmalfeldt, the technique involves three steps: (1) the music tries to cadence, (2) the attempted cadence is evaded, and (3) the music retries the cadence.

2300.definition: A technique of internal phrase expansion. It occurs when new material causes a phrase to deviate from its expected trajectory toward the cadence. These deviations may be permanent ("reroutes") or temporary ("detours").

2302.definition: Making a phrase last longer than we expect by lengthening it after it begins, but before it cadences.

2303.definition: Lengthening a phrase by adding extra material to it either before it begins ("prefix") or after it cadences ("suffix").

2322.definition: A type of form that has two core sections. These sections are often called "reprises" because each is typically repeated. There are two main types of binary form: rounded and simple.

2329.definition: A retransition is very similar to a transition, but retransitions lead to a return to the main section in the tonic key, while transitions move away from tonic. Retransitions may have a clear half-cadential ending (possibly followed by a suffix), or they may have an elided ending that coincides with the initiation of the following section.

2332.definition: A section of music that functions to connect two thematic sections, especially where the upcoming section is not the initiation of a large-scale return.

2334.definition: A large suffix section occurring at the end of a work (or end of a movement within a multi-movement work), after the PAC that ends the piece’s core sections.

2358.definition: The overlapping of two phrases, functioning as the ending of one phrase and the simultaneous beginning of the next.

2363.definition: A section of music that occurs before the start of the first core section.

2367.definition: The process of becoming is an analytical phenomenon that captures an in-time, analytical reinterpretation regarding a formal/phrasal unit's function, abbreviated with a rightward double arrow symbol (⇒). Examples include primary theme ⇒ transition, continuation ⇒ cadential, or suffix ⇒ transition.

2411.definition: Substituting a major I chord for a minor I chord (for example, using C major instead of C minor in a piece that is in C minor overall).

2414.definition: A type of alternative path. A detour creates a temporary deviation from a phrase's expected trajectory toward a cadence. Detours are initiated by a diversion onto the detour and they end with a resumption of rhetoric from earlier in the phrase.

2415.definition: A type of alternative path that involves a permanent change of a phrase's trajectory toward the cadence. Reroutes are initiated by a diversion.

2423.definition: An external expansion that occurs before the beginning of a phrase. Prefixes are usually introductions, and they may be small, as when the accompaniment for a lied begins before the singer, or they may be large, as when a symphony begins with a slow introduction.

2424.definition: A type of external expansion that occurs after the end of a phrase. There are three terms commonly used to describe suffixes, ranging in size from smaller to larger: post-cadential extension, codetta, and coda.

2458.definition: A chromatic chord that temporarily tonicizes another key besides the tonic key, by taking on a dominant function in that new key.

2488.definition: A type of suffix (external expansion). Post-cadential extensions are usually short, they often occur at the ends of phrases within a section, and they typically prolong the final chord of the cadence or re-state the two chords that created the cadence.

2489.definition: A type of suffix (external expansion). Codettas are usually medium length (for example, between 4 and 8 measures), they often occur at the end of a section within a piece, and they often feature repeated units. They may or may not contain a full phrase.

2533.definition: A discrete tone with an individual frequency.

2535.definition: A group of pitches that are octave equivalent and enharmonically equivalent.

2564.definition: ♭VII–I, or B♭–C in C major. This shuttle can imply mixolydian if the tonic chord is major, or aeolian if it is minor. In this shuttle, the ♭VII chord has dominant function.

2565.definition: i–♭VII–♭VI–♭VII. This progression can be understood as a shuttle between i and ♭VI, with the intermediate ♭VIIs acting as passing chords.

2566.definition: ♭VI–♭VII–i, or A♭–B♭–Cmi in C minor. This schema implies the aeolian mode. Very frequently, the i chord is altered to be major, yielding a sequence of three major chords related by steps in the same direction. This progression, especially with a major I chord, is often associated with heroic themes in video games and movies.

2567.definition: A harmonization of a descending upper tetrachord (1̂–7̂–6̂–5̂) in the bass.

2568.definition: IV–i, or F–Cmi in C minor. This shuttle implies the dorian mode. It can sound like ii–V to someone who is not used to the dorian mode.

2569.definition: I–II♯, or C–D in C major. This progression can easily be confused with IV–V in major or ♭VII–I in mixolydian, so one should be careful when referencing this progression. It implies the lydian mode.

2588.definition: An interval of twelve half steps between two notes with the same letter name. The frequencies of two notes related by octave form a 2:1 ratio. Abbreviated “8ve.”

2643.definition: A performance practice in which two notated eighth notes are performed unequally, in about a 2:1 proportion.

2644.definition: Eighth notes that are equal, as opposed to swing eighths (which are unequal).

2649.definition: An accent on beats 2 and 4 of a quadruple meter. Backbeats are common in jazz and pop styles.

2650.definition: A rhythmic phenomenon in which the hierarchy of the underlying meter is contradicted through surface rhythms. Syncopation is usually created through accents and/or longer durations.

2685.definition: In jazz, the piano, guitar, bass, and percussion.

2686.definition: A type of jazz/pop score that typically notates only the melody and the chord symbols (written above the staff).

2698.definition: An interval that is larger than an octave.

2699.definition: Adding additional thirds on top of the triad. Most commonly refers to ninths, elevenths, or thirteenths rather than sevenths, although sevenths are also extensions.

2719.definition: Spelling chords stacked in thirds or in closed position, within a single staff, usually for abstract or theoretical purposes, rather than for performance.

2721.definition: Distribution of notes in a chord into idiomatic registers for performance.

2722.definition: Duplicating some notes of a chord in multiple parts.

2725.definition: A unit of measurement for the frequency of a sound, equivalent to one cycle per second.

2726.definition: An overtone of a complex sound that occurs at a whole-number ratio to the fundamental.

2728.definition: A component frequency within a complex tone's set of overtones.

2729.definition: Any one of several bass-range string instruments, including the double bass (upright bass, string bass, contrabass, acoustic bass) or the bass guitar (electric or acoustic).

2734.definition: The way a specific voice within a larger texture moves when the harmonies change. For example, in a choir with four parts, soprano/alto/tenor/bass, one might discuss the voice leading in the tenor part as the entire choir moves from I to V.

2735.definition: A tone that is present in more than one chord.

2770.definition: Relating in some sense to the chromatic scale. The term may be used to refer to notes that are outside the given key.

2771.definition:
1. A scale, mode, or collection that follows the pattern of whole and half steps W–W–H–W–W–W–H, or any rotation of that pattern.
2. Belonging to the local key (as opposed to "chromatic").

2772.definition: A chord from another key inserted into a new key, in order to tonicize a diatonic chord other than I.

2811.definition: A kind of inconclusive cadence that occurs when a phrase ends on V. Occasionally, particularly in Romantic music, the final chord of a half cadence will be V⁷.

2819.definition: The distance between two pitches measured in semitones, with a plus or minus symbol to indicate ascending or descending, respectively. For example: C₄ to E₅ would be an ordered pitch interval of +16.

2820.definition: The distance between two pitches, measured in semitones. For example, C₄ to E₅ would be an unordered pitch interval of 16.

2822.definition: The distance between pitch classes from lowest to highest. In other words, pitch class intervals are measured on the clock face, always going clockwise.

2823.definition: Unordered pitch-class intervals; that is, the smallest possible distance in semitones between two pitch classes. Thus, mi2 and ma7 are both IC 1; ma2, mi7, +6 are IC 2; mi3, ma6, +2 are IC 3, etc. The largest interval class is six semitones, because if order is disregarded, the tritone is the largest possible interval.

2845.definition: ii⁷–V⁷–Imaj⁷ in major, or iiø⁷–V⁷–i⁷ in minor. A fundamentally important progression in traditional jazz.

2846.definition: A term that summarizes the quality of the third, fifth, and seventh (if applicable) above the root of the chord. Common chord qualities are major, minor, diminished, half-diminished, dominant, and augmented.

2847.definition: A seventh chord in which the triad quality is minor and the seventh quality is also minor. For example: C–E♭–G–B♭.

2848.definition: A seventh chord in which the triad quality is major and the seventh quality is minor.

2850.definition: A seventh chord in which the triad quality is diminished and the seventh quality is minor.

2869.definition: A V–I cadence that ends with do (1̂) in the melody. Both harmonies must be in root position.

2872.definition: A V–I cadence in which V, I, or both harmonies are inverted, and/or do (1̂) is not in the soprano over the tonic triad. Additionally, IACs are often used to evade a cadence.

2989.definition: A complex large-scale musical form that can be understood as an elaborate version of rounded binary form with a balanced component. The larger level names are as follows: Exposition (≈A), Development (≈B), and Recapitulation (≈A′). In general terms, the exposition contains two main sections (primary and secondary) separated by a transition. The secondary theme is presented in a non-tonic key in the exposition, and crucially, it is restated in the recapitulation in the tonic key. The exposition and recapitulation often end with a large suffix (closing section).

2992.definition: The intermixing of major and minor versions of 3̂, 6̂, and/or 7̂ within a composition.

3000.definition: A type of motion where a chord tone moves by step to another tone, then moves back to the original chord tone. For example, C–D–C above a C major chord would be an example of neighboring motion, in which D can be described as a neighbor tone. Entire harmonies may be said to be neighboring when embellishing another harmony, when the voice-leading between the two chords involves only neighboring and common-tone motion (as in the common-tone diminished seventh chord).

3030.definition: The moment when the tail end of the first reprise returns at the tail end of the second reprise of a binary or sonata form.

3048.definition: One of three formal functions (with the other two being middle and ending). Beginnings are often signaled by establishment of a new melody or repetition of the beginning of a previously heard melody, emphasis on tonic harmony (especially root position), a melody that opens up musical space by ascending, a statement of a motive that is developed through the remainder of the phrase.

3049.definition: Occurs when a potential cadence point is declined by the material that follows it. A common strategy is for a composer to write music that proposes a cadence, but then to "back up" in the phrase and try the cadence again. See also the "one-more-time" technique in the chapter on phrase expansion.

3064.definition: A tone that exists outside of the twelve-tone equal-tempered scale (for example, quarter tones).

3078.definition: A feature of musical phrasing that features a simulated dialogue between two instruments or groups of instruments.

3080.definition: Notes whose exact pitch sounds somewhere between the flat and regular versions of a scale degree, particularly 3̂ and 7̂.

3081.definition: A pentatonic scale with the intervals mi3–ma2–ma2–mi3–ma2. For example, starting on A, the minor pentatonic would be A–C–D–E–G. The minor pentatonic is a rotation of the major pentatonic.

3082.definition: A scale that proceeds ma2–ma2–mi3–ma2–mi3. For example, starting on C, the C major pentatonic scale is C–D–E–G–A.

3161.definition: A formal category including both main sections (e.g., A, primary theme, refrain) and contrasting sections (e.g., B, C, D, secondary theme, episode, contrasting middle, development, digression). In contrast to auxiliary sections, core sections present the main musical material of a work and generally represent the bulk of a composition.

3167.definition: Repeated chord progressions, often four bars long, that are repeated throughout a portion or all of a song.

3230.definition: A group of lyrics that is four lines long.

3231.definition: In lyrics, a stanza is a group of lines of lyrics. In music notation, a stanza is a group of staves that are played simultaneously.

3297.definition: Use of a minor iv chord in a major key. This creates a semitone descent between scale degrees ↓6̂ and 5̂. It is common to precede iv with IV (major), creating a descent 6̂–↓6̂–5̂.

3487.definition: An instrument that produces sound via one or more vibrating strings.

3557.definition: A relationship between pitches that share a letter name but are separated by one or more octaves.

3628.definition: The number of scale steps between notes of a collection or scale.

3728.definition: Occurs when the tonic is never actually sounded as a harmony during the song, but is still implied through the melody or through the use of conventional harmonic progressions.

3848.definition: A single step within a scale; usually indicated by either a solfège syllable or an Arabic numeral with a caret.

3850.definition: A system of naming pitch classes that treats C as 0, C♯ as 1, D as 2, etc.

3858.definition: Ordering the notes of a chord so that it is entirely stacked in thirds. The root of the chord is on the bottom.

3859.definition: The most compressed way to write a given collection of pitch classes.

3860.definition: An integer x's complement mod 12 is the number y that would sum to 12. For example, 11's complement mod 12 is 1.

3889.definition: A group of pitch-class sets related by transposition or inversion. Set classes are named by their prime forms; for example, (012) is a set class.

3890.definition: A name for a set class. The prime form is the version of the set class that is most compact to the left and transposed to begin on 0.

3894.definition: The number of elements in a set or other grouping.

3895.definition: A nomenclature for set classes developed by Allen Forte; each set class has a unique Forte number. The first number refers to the cardinality of the set, and the second number is semi-arbitrary, but generally proceeds from the most compact to the most expanded set.

3949.definition: The act of moving pitch content by a certain interval.

3950.definition: The act of mirroring pitch content vertically, so that motion down becomes up and up becomes down. Inversion often preserves intervallic content.

3951.definition: In set theory, a class is a group whose members are all equivalent in some sense—transposition, inversion, octave, enharmonic, etc.

3952.definition: In set theory, a group whose members are not necessarily related.

3954.definition: A larger set that contains other smaller sets. For example, a superset of (037) is the diatonic collection, (013568t).

3955.definition: Music that is atonal, avoiding a traditional pitch center and harmonic hierarchy, but is not serial.

3999.definition: In a transformation (Tₙ or Iₙ), n is the index number, representing the interval of transposition in semitones.

4000.definition: Short for modulo 12, where numbers wrap around upon reaching 12. Arithmetic in mod 12 is most commonly encountered in clock time: after 12 o’clock, the time becomes 1 o’clock again.

4102.definition: Getting gradually louder; sometimes represented in notated scores with a hairpin symbol.

4103.definition: Getting gradually softer; sometimes represented in notated scores with a hairpin symbol.

4119.definition: Refers to both a note's length and the accent level of its attack.

4120.definition: The onset of a note (as opposed to the following sustain or decay).

4126.definition: How fast or slow a work is performed; many tempo markings are in Italian or another non-English language.

4139.definition: To divide time into different periods.

4143.definition: Musical features that pertain to section divisions and form.

4144.definition: A symbol that indicates one should hold a note longer than its written duration. Notation: 𝄐

4145.definition: Indicates a break and/or a cutoff.

4146.definition: Indicates a breath (for wind instrumentalists and vocalists) or a pause (for percussionists and string players).

4147.definition: Symbols (𝄆 and 𝄇) indicating that a section of music is repeated.

4174.definition: The home note or home chord of a scale, or something with the function of that home note.

4175.definition: In church modes, the final loosely corresponds to the modern notion of "tonic," in that it is a melodic goal. However, the final may not always be emphasized in the way a tonic is. Finals are named by the fact that the last note of a Gregorian chant will always be the final of the mode.

4176.definition: In church modes, authentic modes are those that range from final to final.

4177.definition: A mode with a range of a fifth above and fourth below its tonic.

4232.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern W–W–H–W–W–H–W. This is like the major scale, but with a lowered 7̂. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on G.

4233.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern W–W–W–H–W–W–H. This is like the major scale, but with a raised 4̂. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on F.

4234.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern W–H–W–W–H–W–W. This is like the natural minor scale. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on A.

4235.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern W–H–W–W–W–H–W. This is like the natural minor scale, but with a raised 6̂. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on D.

4236.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern H–W–W–W–H–W–W. This is like the natural minor scale, but with a lowered 2̂. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on E.

4238.definition: Considered in relation to some other system. For example, modes are said to be relative if their scales share all the same notes (like C major and A minor).

4265.definition: A pitch collection composed entirely of whole steps. There are six whole steps in a whole tone collection, and there are only two possible whole tone scales: C–D–E–F♯–G♯–A♯, or C♯–D♯–F–G–A–B.

4266.definition: A pitch collection built with the interval pattern ma2–ma2–mi3–ma2–mi3. This collection can also be generated by using scale degrees 1̂, 2̂, 3̂, 5̂, and 6̂ only of the major scale.

4267.definition: Pandiatonicism uses the notes of a diatonic collection without imparting a sense of pitch center.

4268.definition: The octatonic collection is built with an alternation of whole steps and half steps, leading to a total of eight distinct pitches. One example is C–C♯–D♯–E–F♯–G–A–B♭. Jazz musicians refer to this as the diminished scale.

4294.definition: Describes when a theme, row form, or motive is played backward in comparison to an initial (or original) statement.

4334.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that preserves the major third in the triad and moves the remaining note by whole tone (e.g., relating C major and A minor).

4335.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that preserves the perfect fifth in the triad, and moves the remaining note by semitone (e.g., relating C major and C minor).

4336.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that preserves the minor third in the triad, and moves the remaining note by semitone (e.g., relating C major and E minor).

4337.definition: A six-note collection that alternates between half steps and minor thirds, such as C–C♯–E–F–G♯–A.

4338.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that moves the two pitches that form the perfect fifth in a triad by semitone and changes the mode of the triad (e.g., relating C major and C♯ minor).

4339.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that moves both members of the minor third in a triad by semitone, and again changes the mode (e.g., relating C major and F minor).

4340.definition: A Neo-Riemannian transformation that connects a triad to its modal opposite a third away by moving each voice by a single semitone (e.g., connecting C major and A♭ minor).

4458.definition: A ternary form whose sections are each made up of one or more phrases but not complete forms. The term "simple" can also be used to clarify that a single section does not contain a complete form. Compare with compound ternary form.

4531.definition: A curved line placed over notes to indicate that they should be played or sung without separation.

4533.definition: Played or sung with more separation, leaving space between notes.

4547.definition: To play with a more forceful accent or emphasis.

4585.definition: Designates specific musical frequencies by combining a note name (such as C) with an octave designation (such as 4), creating a bipartite label (C₄).

4629.definition: A note value that lasts the duration of two half notes. Notation: 𝅝

4630.definition: A note value that lasts half the duration of a whole note, or the duration of two quarter notes. Notation: 𝅗𝅥

4631.definition: A note value that lasts half the duration of a half note, or the duration of two eighth notes. Notation: 𝅘𝅥

4632.definition: A note value that lasts half the duration of a quarter note, or the duration of two sixteenth notes. Notation: 𝅘𝅥𝅮

4633.definition: A note value that lasts half the duration of an eighth note. Notation: 𝅘𝅥𝅯

4635.definition: A type of rest that lasts the duration of two half rests. Notation: 𝄻

4636.definition: A type of rest that lasts half the duration of a whole rest, or the duration of two quarter rests. Notation: 𝄻

4637.definition: A type of rest that lasts half the duration of a half rest, or the duration of two eighth rests. Notation: 𝄽

4638.definition: A type of rest that lasts half the duration of a quarter rest, or the duration of two sixteenth rests. Notation: 𝄾

4639.definition: A type of rest that lasts half the duration of an eighth rest. Notation: 𝄿

4640.definition: Increases a note or rest value by half.

4641.definition: Connects two or more notes of the same pitch; notes after the initial one are not rearticulated.

4646.definition: A recurring pattern of accents that occur over time. Meters are indicated in music notation with a time signature.

4650.definition: The relative duration of a note.

4663.definition: A note value that lasts the duration of two whole notes. Notation: 𝅜

4673.definition: A measured silence in a piece of music.

4701.definition: An indication of tempo in beats per minute (BPM).

4725.definition: A meter that divides the beat into two parts.

4726.definition: A pulse in music to which one can tap or clap along. A grouped hierarchy of beats forms a meter.

4734.definition: A meter with two beats per measure.

4735.definition: A meter with three beats per measure.

4736.definition: A meter with four beats per measure.

4738.definition: A meter with two beats, each of which divides into two. The top number of a simple duple meter will always be "2". 2/4 and 2/2 (cut time, 𝄵) are the most common simple duple meters.

4740.definition: A meter with three beats, each of which divides into two. The top number of a simple triple meter will always be "3". 3/4 is the most common compound triple meter.

4742.definition: A meter with four beats, each of which divides into two. The top number of a simple quadruple meter will always be "4". 4/4 (common time, 𝄴) is the most common compound quadruple meter.

4767.definition: An indication of meter in Western music notation, often made up of two numbers stacked vertically.

4769.definition: Created by bar lines, a measure (or bar) is equivalent to one beat grouping.

4786.definition: Beat 1 of a measure, which is conducted with a downward motion.

4788.definition: The last beat of a measure which is conducted with an upward motion.

4790.definition: Which note value gets the beat (e.g., the quarter note in 4/4 or the dotted quarter note in 6/8).

4803.definition: Notes on an upbeat that lead into the first downbeat of a phrase.

4862.definition: A meter that divides the beat into three parts.

4863.definition: The note value that divides the beat into two or three parts (in simple or compound meters, respectively); for example, the eighth note in 4/4 or 6/8.

5001.definition: A tuplet that involves dividing a beat in simple meter into three parts.

5003.definition: A rhythm that involves dividing the beat into a different number of subdivisions from that usually implied by the time signature.

5014.definition: A tuplet that involves dividing a beat in compound meter into two parts.

5024.definition: Groupings of measures into different patterns of accentuation akin to meter. A hypermeasure is typically four measures long.

5036.definition: A rhythmic or note value that does not fall on a beat (1, 2, 3, etc.).

5061.definition: A system of musical notation stripped of complicating elements, focusing only on basic elements of meter, rhythm, and scale degree.

5068.definition: An ordered collection of half steps and whole steps.

5072.definition: An ordered collection of half steps (H) and whole steps (W) as follows (ascending): W–W–H–W–W–W–H.

5131.definition: The relative position of a note within a diatonic scale. Indicated with a number, 1–7, that indicates this position relative to the tonic of that scale.

5132.definition: A symbol akin to an angled bracket, placed above Arabic numerals to indicate scale degrees; a circumflex symbol.

5136.definition: The application of solmization syllables (do, re, mi, fa, sol, etc.) to scale degrees.

5139.definition: A system of solfège in which do is the first scale degree in a scale; this is in contrast to fixed do, where do is always the pitch class C.

5141.definition: A system of solfège in which do is always the pitch class C, re the pitch class D, etc., regardless of scale.

5142.definition: A system that pairs each note of a scale with a particular syllable.

5147.definition: A movable system of names for scale degrees based on their function within the scale, such as tonic (do, 1̂) and dominant (sol, 5̂).

5205.definition: In music notation, a collection of sharps or flats written at the beginning of each line (immediately after the clef) to signal that certain notes are always sharp/flat.

5232.definition: A graphic that shows the relationship between major (and/or minor) key signatures by placing the key signatures around a circle in order of number of accidentals.

5272.definition: A collection of notes that consists of twelve half steps.

5294.definition: An ordered collection of half steps (H) and whole steps (W) with the ascending succession W–H–W–W–H–W–W.

5295.definition: An ordered collection of half and whole steps with the ascending succession W–H–W–W–H–3Hs–H. Like natural minor, but with a raised 7̂.

5296.definition: An ordered collection of half steps (H) and whole steps (W) with the ascending succession W–H–W–W–W–W–H and the descending succession W–W–H–W–W–H–W.

5367.definition: When two keys/scales share the same tonic, such as C major and C minor.

5370.definition: When two keys/scales share the same pitches.

5453.definition: Refers to three categories of chords: tonic, predominant, and dominant. A chord's membership within a category indicates something about how that chord typically behaves in tonal harmonic progressions in Western classical music. For example, tonic function chords are stable and tend to represent points of resolution or repose.

5456.definition: Predominant function chords are those that transition away from tonic function toward dominant function.

5461.definition: Indicates the typical order and flow of harmonic functions in a phrase: tonic–predominant–dominant(–tonic).

5603.definition: "Bright" refers to a more major sound, while "dark" refers to a more minor sound.

5609.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern W–W–H–W–W–W–H. This is equivalent to a major scale.

5632.definition: A diatonic mode that follows the pattern H–W–W–H–W–W–W. This is like the natural minor scale, but with a lowered 2̂ and lowered 5̂. This scale can also be found by playing the white notes of the piano starting on B.

5682.definition: Singing music at "sight" (that is, never having seen it before).

5685.definition: Counting at "sight" (that is, never having seen or heard the rhythm before).

5699.definition: A type of aural skills exercise in which aural examples are written by the student in staff notation.

5703.definition: An abbreviated form of musical rhythmic notation, that involves dashes to indicate articulations, horizontal lines to indicate a sustained note, and circles to indicate rests.

5706.definition: Lines that indicate whether pitch moves up, down, or stays the same.

5755.definition: Notes that decorate other, more structurally important notes. Embellishing tones are often not part of the prevailing chord. Types of embellishing tones include passing tones, neighbor tones, appoggiaturas, escape tones, pedal tones, suspensions, and anticipations.

5756.definition: A type of motion where a chord tone moves by step to another tone, then resolves by step in the same direction. For example, C–D–E above a C major chord would be an example of neighboring motion, in which D can be described as a passing tone. Entire harmonies may be said to be passing when embellishing another harmony, when the voice-leading between the two chords involves mainly passing tones (as in the passing 6/4 chord).

5757.definition: Embellishing tones that are approached by step and left by step in the opposite direction.

5760.definition: An embellishing tone often occurring on a strong beat that is approached by leap and left by step in the opposite direction.

5761.definition: An embellishing tone that is approached by step and left by leap in the opposite direction.

5792.definition: An embellishing tone that is approached via static note and left by step down. The suspension is on a strong part of the beat.

5794.definition: An embellishing tone that is approached by static note and left by step up. The retardation is on a stronger part of the beat.

5795.definition: Pedal tones are often found in the bass. They consist of a series of static notes over top of which chord changes occur that do not include the bass.

5797.definition: A two-note embellishing tone gesture in which a chord tone is heard early as a non-chord tone.

5894.definition: When a given harmony’s influence lasts longer than a single chord. Usually this is accomplished by alternating the prolonged chord with other, less important chords.

5895.definition:
1. Write the entire bass
2. Write the entire soprano to make a smooth melody that interacts well with the bass. Choose active notes for the soprano above dominant-function chords, and remember you do not always need to write left to right.
3. Write the inner voices by asking, "What notes do I already have? What notes do I still need? Considering spacing and resolution, what note placement would give me the smoothest motion?"

5934.definition: A 6/4 chord built on a passing tone in the bass, most commonly found prolonging tonic or predominant harmonies. Importantly, the chords on both sides of the passing 6/4 are always the same function.

5971.definition: Occurs when IV (or IV⁶) moves to I (or I⁶).

5988.definition: The phrygian half cadence (PHC) is a special kind of cadential phrase ending that occurs only in minor and involves the progression iv6–V. It's called “phrygian” because of the half step that occurs when le (↓6̂) moves to sol (5̂) in the bass, a sound that’s similar to when ra (↓2̂) moves to do (1̂) in the phrygian mode.

6040.definition: Refers to the 7th of a chord. For example, V7 in the key of C is spelled G-B-D-F. The note F is the chordal 7th. We say chordal 7th to distinguish it from the leading-tone (Ti, [latex]\hat{7}[/latex]).

6048.definition:
In strict four-voice writing:

1) Approach the chordal seventh by step or common tone

2) Resolve the chordal seventh down by step

Reminder: the chordal seventh is different from the leading tone.

6057.definition: An interval whose notes are sounded separately (one note after another).

6058.definition: An interval whose notes sound together (simultaneously).

6062.definition: The number of letters (or lines and spaces) that make up the span of an interval. Interval size is written with Arabic numbers (2, 3, 4, etc.).

6074.definition: The segment of music that establishes the pattern for a sequence; in other words, the segment that gets copied in a sequence.

6075.definition: The segment of a sequence that repeats and transposes the material from the model.

6087.definition: Intervals that are one half step larger than a perfect or major interval.

6101.definition: Intervals that are one half step smaller than a perfect or minor interval.

6104.definition: Occurs when two notes are flipped: for instance, C below E is an inversion of E below C.

6114.definition: A leading-tone chord that makes a non-tonic chord temporarily sound like tonic. Most often, secondary leading-tone chords are fully diminished, though occasionally they are half-diminished.

6196.definition: As an acoustic phenomenon, frequencies vibrating at whole-number ratios with one another; as a cultural phenomenon, perceived stability in a chord or interval.

6197.definition: A perceived quality of auditory roughness in an interval or chord.

6330.definition: Any combination of two or more pitch classes that sound simultaneously.

6332.definition: A three-note chord whose pitch classes can be arranged as thirds.

6335.definition: A chord spacing in which the chord fits within one octave.

6336.definition: The lowest note of a triad or seventh chord when the chord is stacked in thirds.

6429.definition: A variety of harmonic progressions that harmonize a stepwise descending bass line from tonic to dominant. The simplest diatonic version uses the bass notes do–te–le–sol and is harmonized by the progression i–v⁶–iv⁶–V. Chromatic alternatives are common.

6448.definition: A triad whose third is major and fifth is perfect.

6449.definition: A triad whose third is minor and fifth is perfect.

6450.definition: A triad whose third is minor and fifth is diminished.

6451.definition: A triad whose third is major and fifth is augmented.

6710.definition: A series of notes whose frequencies are multiples of the first frequency: 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, 1:5, etc. Starting with the pitch C₂, this would result in the series of pitches C₂, C₃, G₃, C₄, E₄, G₄, B♭₄, C₅, etc.

6713.definition: A diminished seventh chord that, instead of having dominant function, is a neighbor chord that embellishes the chord that comes after it. The CT°⁷ has a common tone with the root of the following chord; all the other notes are a step away from a note in the following chord.

6723.definition: The minor blues differs from the standard 12-bar blues by having minor seventh chords on the i and iv chords, and replacing the V–IV–I cadence with a ii–V–I cadence.

6724.definition: The jazz blues incorporates several alterations to the 12-bar blues to blend together blues harmony and jazz harmony. In the eighth bar, instead of remaining on tonic, there is an applied ii–V that leads to the ii chord in bar 9. In the third phrase, the V–IV–I of the standard blues is replaced with a ii–V–I more common to jazz.

6757.definition: A temporary key within a piece that is overall in a different key. For example, a piece in A major may temporarily modulate to E major; E major is a secondary key within A major.

7055.definition: Notes played or sung all together at the same time.

7115.definition: Imitation sees two or more parts enter separately with (versions of) the same melody.

7121.definition: The first part of a fugue, in which each voice states the subject or answer.

7123.definition: A short melody that forms the melodic basis of a fugue and recurs throughout.

7143.definition: The lowest part (or "voice") of a composition.

7150.definition: Arabic numerals and symbols that indicate intervals above a bass note. These are realized into chords and non-chord tones by musicians.

7151.definition: The process of turning figured bass symbols into chords.

7153.definition: Changing the bass note of a harmony so that, for example, the third is in the bass instead of the root.

7155.definition: Notes of a chord are spaced out beyond their closest possible position.

7268.definition: A musical texture with a single, unaccompanied melodic line.

7270.definition: A musical texture with multiple simultaneous variants on a single melodic line.

7272.definition: A musical texture consisting of one melodic part (usually the topmost) and other subordinate accompanying parts. This includes chorale texture and melody-and-accompaniment texture.

7273.definition: A musical texture with multiple independent melodic voices, distinguished from one another through different rhythms and/or intervallic profiles. Also known as counterpoint. Polyphony may occur in many styles but is commonly associated with contrapuntal genres like fugues and canons.

7298.definition: A triad with an additional third above the fifth, creating a seventh between that top note and the bass and totaling four notes.

7299.definition: Refers to the seventh above the root of a chord. For example, V⁷ in the key of C is spelled G-B-D-F; F is the chordal seventh.

7300.definition: A seventh chord with a major triad and a major seventh. Also known as a major seventh chord.

7301.definition: A seventh chord with a major triad and a minor seventh. Also known as a dominant seventh chord.

7302.definition: A seventh chord with a minor triad and a minor seventh. Also known as a minor seventh chord.

7304.definition: A seventh chord whose triad is diminished and whose seventh is diminished.

7305.definition: A seventh chord with a major triad and a major seventh.

7306.definition: A seventh chord with a minor triad and a minor seventh.

7308.definition: Another name for a fully diminished seventh chord, a seventh chord with a diminished triad and a diminished seventh.

7405.definition: A stress or emphasis on a note.

7439.definition: A clef used by non-pitched percussion instruments, where each line or space is dedicated to a different sound. Notation: 𝄥

7527.definition: The density of and interaction between voices in a work.

7542.definition: A type of homophony in which one can clearly distinguish between melodic and supporting voices, usually with differing rhythms between them.

7614.definition: A phrase that differs substantially from the archetypal sentence while still exhibiting some traits of a sentence-structure phrase.

7902.definition: A chord in which all the notes are played simultaneously.

7975.definition: Any situation where a composer sets up the expectation for a cadence, then avoids cadencing. Examples include deceptive motion, inversion of the cadential dominant or tonic, and/or omitting an essential voice (such as the bass note of the tonic chord or the soprano note of the tonic chord).

8423.definition: A strategy of putting elements of music (pitch, duration, dynamics, etc.) in a particular order.

8425.definition: Refers to the ordered elements in a serial composition. These elements are often pitches, but could be other things such as durations or dynamics.

8426.definition: The ordered elements in a serial composition, also referred to as a series. These elements are often pitches, but could be other things such as durations or dynamics.

8428.definition: A collection of all forms of a given row. Most row classes contain 48 versions of a row, but some contain fewer due to duplications of row forms. For example, a prime version of a row may be equivalent to a retrograde version of the row.

8434.definition: A six-note collection. In serial music, "hexachord" is typically used to refer to either the first or last six notes of a twelve-tone row.

8436.definition: A particular version of a row in serial music; that is, prime, transposed, inverted, or retrograded.

8438.definition: A portion of a larger grouping. In serial analysis, segments of a row can be any number of elements (for example, in a twelve-tone row, it's common to look at three- or four-note segments).

8439.definition: A twelve-tone row that contains all eleven ordered pitch-class intervals.

8444.definition: In serial music, invariance refers to keeping a property of a row the same through different transformations. For example, when a retrograde version of a row contains the same ordered pitch classes as a prime version of the row, we would call it "retrograde invariant" to mean that the order of pitch classes doesn't change when the row is reversed and transposed

8451.definition: A property of a row in which combining one hexachord from a version of a row with a hexachord from another version of a row creates the chromatic collection.

8456.definition: The first large section in a sonata-form work. It usually establishes the main themes of a work and sets up a conflict that is later resolved in the work. This conflict often takes the form of differing key centers (such as when the primary theme of a sonata is in tonic and the secondary theme is in the dominant).

8457.definition: A section of a sonata form that is unstable, and that may or may not explore thematic material established in the exposition.

8458.definition: A section of a sonata-form work that brings back themes from the exposition and resolves the conflict established in the exposition.

8584.definition: In typesetting, superscript characters appear higher on the page than the regular characters—like an exponent in math. For example, in the chord symbol C⁷, the 7 is superscript.

8590.definition: Existing on its own, without reference to another system. For example, "absolute pitch" refers to the phenomenon of being able to sing a pitch without referencing an instrument or another pitch.

8725.definition: A 12-by-12 grid that sets out all 48 forms of a row class.

8751.definition: Musica ficta are un-notated accidentals added to Renaissance music. Competent performers know to add ficta in appropriate places. In modern editions of Renaissance music, ficta are often provided by the editor.

8991.definition: A triadic harmony with the third in the bass.

8992.definition: A triadic harmony with the fifth in the bass.

9005.definition: A methodology for analyzing pitch in atonal music. Pitch classes are given an integer name (0–11, where C is 0, C♯ is 1, etc.). Groups of pitches are considered together as "sets." Sets may be related by inversion or transposition.

9006.definition: In set theory, "operations" refers to transposition and inversion.

9041.definition: When a single voice of the musical texture bridges what would otherwise be a gap between two sections.

9389.definition:
A system of naming chords that specifies the note name of the root, chord quality, and any alterations.

Some basic symbols are given below as a quick reference, but for more detail, see the Chord Symbols chapter.
