9492.definition: Labeling chords with Roman numerals (and, often, figures).

9506.definition: Numerals I, II, III, IV, V, VI, and VII for 1–7, respectively. In the analysis of harmony, Roman numerals represent triads built on the corresponding scale degree (for example, a V chord is a triad built on 5̂).

9512.definition: A periodization of Western music utilized by music theorists and musicologists encompassing c. 1600–1900.

9702.definition: A musical texture with soprano (S), alto (A), tenor (T), and bass (B) parts.

9776.definition: On a grand staff in SATB style, the soprano and tenor are up-stemmed, while the alto and bass are down-stemmed.

9778.definition: The pitch content of a chord.

9782.definition: The intervals between voices. For chords in strict SATB style, there should be no more than an octave between upper voices (soprano and alto, alto and tenor), and no more than a twelfth between the tenor and bass.

9784.definition: When a higher voice part moves below a lower voice part. In strict SATB style, the ranges of voices should not cross; the soprano must always be higher than the alto, the alto must always be higher than the tenor, and the tenor must be higher than the bass.

9787.definition: The highest part in SATB style, written in the treble clef staff with an up-stem; its generally accepted range is C₄–G₅.

9789.definition: The second-highest voice part in SATB style, written in the treble clef staff with a down-stem; its generally accepted range is G₃–D₅.

9791.definition: The second lowest part in SATB style, written in the bass clef staff with up-stems; its generally accepted range is C₃–G₄.

9793.definition: The lowest voice in SATB style, written in the bass clef staff with a down-stem; its generally accepted range is F₂–D₄.

9891.definition: A triadic harmony with the chordal seventh in the bass.

10148.definition: A traditional approach to composition pedagogy focused on counterpoint as a way of learning to think of music horizontally (melodically) and vertically (harmonically) simultaneously. Consists of five “species,” each of which focuses on a single compositional element.

10156.definition: Literally meaning “fixed voice," this is a pre-existing melodic line that serves as the basis for a new counterpoint exercise or other composition.

10184.definition: A repeated rhythmic or pitched musical idea.

10186.definition: The first part in a pair of imitative voices (compare to comes).

10187.definition: The second (following) part in a pair of imitative voices (compare to dux).

10221.definition: A set that is entirely contained within another larger set.

10224.definition: A type of interval that is measured in semitones. For example, the pitch interval 2 is two semitones; the pitch interval 7 is seven semitones.

10505.definition: A meter that divides measures into unequal groupings of beats or divisions, creating an uneven metrical pulse.

10573.definition: Music that does not have any perceivable meter

10656.definition: A term for a meter consisting of several rapid time-signature changes.

10717.definition: When two or more meters are notated simultaneously.

10718.definition: A means of smoothing out abrupt tempo changes by introducing subdivisions or groups of beats in the first tempo that match durations in the new tempo.

10773.definition: An acoustic wave (energy vibration) that is perceived as sound.

10774.definition: The distance between two peaks of a sound wave.

10775.definition: Acoustically, how often a sound wave repeats; the pitch of a sound.

10886.definition: A compositional device that begins with a small rhythmic unit and gradually adds length to the durations.

10888.definition: A contemporary metric technique that uses seconds as the measure of time, rather than traditional bar lines and meters.

10891.definition: A gradual change in the speed of notes within a single beam.

11023.definition: A notational technique where pitch and durations are specified by nonstandard symbols.

11102.definition: A system that pairs rhythmic values with particular syllables.

11224.definition: An augmented fourth or diminished fifth. The name reflects that the two notes of a tritone are three (tri-) whole steps (tones) apart.

11265.definition: A type of articulation marking used to indicate smooth, connected playing, indicated by small horizontal lines above or below the notes.

11316.definition: A group of things that appear in a specified sequence. An ordered pitch set, for example, appears in a consistent order within a piece of music. Compare against a pitch class set, where the pitches are unordered, meaning they can appear in any order in the piece of music.

11539.definition: A category of formal sections that connect two core sections; for example, transitions and retransitions.

11541.definition: A section that presents the work's primary musical ideas. Usually, the main section is the first core section of the work. Examples include primary themes, refrains, expositions, choruses, or strophes.

11542.definition: A core section that provides contrast with the main section. May be stable or unstable.

11546.definition: A category of auxiliary sections including prefixes (which introduce a piece/section) and suffixes (which follow the generic conclusion of a piece/section).

11548.definition: A musical form consisting of three distinct sections, in an ABA (not ABC) formal structure. The B section typically contains contrasting material in a new key. Repeat signs around each section are common.

11550.definition: The main section of a sonata-form work, in the tonic key. P themes are usually stable.

11551.definition: The contrasting section of a sonata-form work. The S theme begins and ends in a contrasting key (usually V in major-mode sonatas and either III or v in minor-mode sonatas). S themes are usually stable.

11552.definition: A large suffix in sonata-form works. The closing section is usually very stable and often consists of many V–I or IV–I motions confirming the local tonic.

11554.definition: An intensified version of the chorus that retains the same harmony and contains the hook of the song, which increases memorability for the audience and encourages dancing.

11579.definition: A sonata-form transition that reuses motivic material from the primary theme.

11580.definition: A sonata-form transition that introduces new motivic material (as opposed to reusing material from the primary theme).

11587.definition: In tonal music, a note that has a tendency to move to a specific note in the following chord, usually a step up or down. Also called a "tendency tone."

11601.definition: The triad or seventh chord built on ti (7̂).

11608.definition: A melodic, "horizontal" statement of a triadic harmony; in other words, each note of a triadic harmony played in succession (rather than simultaneously). Also referred to as a "broken chord."

11618.definition: A cadence-like resolution from V to a non-tonic harmony. The most common deceptive motion is V–vi; the next most common is V–IV⁶.

11628.definition: A chord used to modulate between two keys that is diatonic in both.

11659.definition: Extensive prolongation of the V chord. Also known as "standing on the dominant." Often involves a pedal point on sol (5̂).

11661.definition: In sonata form, the cadence that is the goal of the transition and marks the boundary between the transition and the secondary theme. Usually a HC, in I, V, or the secondary key; sometimes an authentic cadence in the secondary key; rarely, it could be an AC in the tonic key.

11662.definition: The goal of the S area. The EEC is the first satisfactory PAC that is followed by new material (not based on S).

11690.definition: A harmony whose function is to prolong another harmony, rather than to advance the phrase toward its cadential goal. Embellishing harmonies are often said to be passing or neighboring.

11692.definition: A type of embellishing tone that is approached by step and left by leap or vice-versa. The name comes from the idea that it functions as a neighbor tone on only one side of its embellishment. Incomplete neighbors may be called appoggiaturas or escape tones.

11700.definition: A common embellishment of the cadential V chord, in which the fifth of the V chord (re, 2̂) is replaced with the sixth (mi/me, 3̂) and the third (ti, 7̂) is replaced with the fourth (do, 1̂). The sixth and fourth form a 6/4 chord, hence its label. The cadential 6/4 resembles a I6/4 in its pitch content.

11701.definition: A kind of 6/4 chord that embellishes a harmony with neighbor motion. This is usually labeled with figures, e.g., with 5-6-5 in one voice and 3-4-3 in another.

11702.definition: A 6/4 chord that results from an arpeggiated bass line (e.g., if the bass line alternates between the root and fifth of the same chord).

11704.definition: The suppression of an expected chord. Two kinds of elision are a leading-tone elision, in which the expected triad is replaced by the dominant seventh chord with the same root or by a functionally equivalent diminished seventh chord, and raised-root elision, in which the root of the expected chord is raised to become a leading tone (or applied leading tone).

11822.definition: Perfect octaves (twelve semitones), perfect unisons (zero semitones), and perfect fifths (seven semitones). Perfect fourths (five semitones) are sometimes considered a perfect consonance, sometimes a dissonance; this depends on the context.

11823.definition: Thirds or sixths with major or minor quality.

11824.definition: When two voices move melodically in opposite directions—that is, one voice moves up and the other moves down.

11825.definition: When two voices move melodically in the same direction (either upward or downward).

11826.definition: When two voices move melodically in the same direction and by the same interval—for example, both voices move upward by a melodic second. (Note: the quality of the interval may vary, and it still counts as parallel motion.) By definition, two voices moving in parallel motion will also maintain the same harmonic interval between them.

11827.definition: When one voice moves melodically while another voice remains on the same pitch.

11831.definition: A melodic interval of a third or greater. Note that some refer to thirds as "skips" rather than leaps.

11836.definition: A general term for music that involves multiple simultaneous and independent melodic lines. The term comes from the idea that each note (point) has another note against (counter to) it. This term can also refer specifically to a musical line added to a cantus firmus.

11837.definition: A general term for two or more sound events occurring at the same time.

11842.definition: In a multi-voice texture, when one voice leaps beyond the previous note in another voice.

11843.definition: Similar motion into a fifth or octave. Also called hidden fifths or octaves.

11846.definition: Passing motion that does not involve dissonance.

11847.definition: In counterpoint, a type of consonant weak beat that involves a leap of a fourth followed by a step in the opposite direction. The name implies that this motion substitutes for a more common passing-tone motion.

11848.definition: In counterpoint, a type of consonant weak-beat motion that is approached by skip (third) and left by step in the same direction.

11850.definition: In counterpoint, a type of consonant weak beat that divides a larger consonant leap (from downbeat to downbeat) into two smaller leaps.

11851.definition: In counterpoint, a type of consonant weak beat that steps in the opposite direction following a large leap.

11852.definition: In counterpoint, a type of consonant weak beat that skips by third and then steps into the following downbeat.

11854.definition: An embellishment that surrounds a note with its upper and lower neighbor (e.g., C–B–D–C). The note being embellished may be articulated between the two neighbor tones, as in C–D–C–B–C.

11855.definition:
A five-note species counterpoint embellishment that may occur in one of two different forms:

1) Down by step, down by third, up by step, up by step
2) Up by step, up by third, down by step, down by step

11857.definition: Two consecutive weak-beat fifths or octaves in fourth species counterpoint; e.g., from two successive 9–8 suspensions.

11860.definition: A contrapuntal cadence in which a perfect octave or unison is approached through contrary motion by step. One line will have re–do (2̂– 1̂) while the other has ti–do (7̂-1̂). This results in the sequence of harmonic intervals sixth–octave, tenth–octave, or third–unison.

11870.definition: An embellishment that indicates to decorate a note with its upper and lower neighbor, in that order. (The opposite order would be an "inverted" turn.) For example, a turn on C would be performed C–D–C–B–C. This embellishment is a specific kind of double neighbor.

11949.definition: A major scale with le (↓6̂) instead of la (6̂): do–re–mi–fa–sol–le–ti–do (1̂–2̂–3̂–4̂–5̂–↓6̂–7̂–1̂).

11993.definition: Taking a series of notes of equal durations, cutting the duration of the first note in half, and shifting the rest early by that half duration.

11994.definition: A division of a rhythmic unit (one beat, two beats, one measure, etc.) into three almost-equal groups, in a 3+3+2 pattern: for example, dividing a half note into two dotted eighth notes and an eighth note.

12010.definition: A four-part phrase structure in popular music: statement, restatement, departure, and conclusion. An srdc structure shares many features with the Classical sentence.

12035.definition: An imitative repetition of a subject that is not an exact transposition of the subject (that is, a real answer) but modifies the intervals to fit within the same key as the original subject. A common modification is to change a perfect fifth do–sol (1̂–5̂) in the subject to a perfect fourth sol–do (5̂–1̂) in the answer. The term "tonal answer" refers to the fact that this preserves the tonal relationships (e.g., between do and sol) instead of preserving intervallic relationships.

12036.definition: A principle of melody writing suggesting that any large leaps that open up a new register ought to be filled in afterward with stepwise motion.

12043.definition: A melodic line that is consistently sounded with (and complements) the subject/answer of a fugue.

12046.definition: A repetition of the fugue's subject, transposed to another pitch level. May be a "real" answer (a literal transposition) or a "tonal" answer (an inexact transposition).

12048.definition: An independent, monophonic part within a piece of music (instrumental or vocal). Each voice may be played by a different instrument, or multiple voices may be played by one instrument (especially in polyphonic instruments like keyboard or guitar).

12052.definition: Persistent rapid note values, especially sixteenth notes. Common in Baroque music.

12053.definition: A fugue subject transposed by fourth/fifth, stated in a second voice in response to the first voice's subject statement.

12054.definition: A passage of a fugue that does not contain a subject statement in any voice.

12084.definition: Contrapuntal writing without any specific thematic content.

12145.definition: An adjective describing music that lacks any sense of tonal center.

12146.definition: An adjective used to describe music that adheres to the Western system of functional harmony.

12154.definition: A chord composed entirely of seconds (major or minor), rather than thirds or any larger interval.

12155.definition: The set that, together with an original set, will make the complete twelve-tone collection. Complements are literal when referring to pitch class sets and abstract when referring to set classes.

12219.definition: A scale made up of the notes of the diatonic collection.

12220.definition: Related to the word "tenuto," the tenor of a mode is the pitch frequently sustained in a chant melody using that mode.

12225.definition: A seven-note collection similar to the mixolydian mode but with fi (↑4̂); corresponds roughly to the lowest partials of the harmonic series.

12296.definition: The complete chromatic collection (i.e., all twelve pitch classes).

12365.definition: A 12-tone tonerow formed of the same pitch class set several time such as 3 tetrachords or 4 trichords.

12757.definition: A term that indicates the exact number of semitones between two pitches in an interval (compare with interval size, which indicates only the number of letters between two pitches). Common interval qualities are major, minor, perfect, augmented, and diminished.

13002.definition: A Latin American guitar-like instrument particularly prevalent in Puerto Rican music.

13025.definition: A simple drum pattern in which the kick drum is played on beats one and three, alternating with the snare on beats two and four, while eighth notes are played on a closed hi-hat. (This description presumes a 4/4 time signature.)

13026.definition: Beats per minute. A standard unit of measurement for tempo.

331.definition: A notational symbol indicating that the affected note should be held 1.5 times as long.

930.definition: Refers to how "high" or "low" a sound is

981.definition: A combination of two or three syllables: typically one stressed syllable, and one or two unstressed syllables.

13028.definition: The perceptual equivalent of a "beat"—the pulse that you might tap your foot or bob your head along to. A tactus is felt, not notated.

13029.definition: A drum pattern where the backbeat is played twice as fast as usual (that is, on the second eighth of each beat, rather than on beats two and four).

13030.definition: In contrast to a double-time or half-time feel, a normal feel occurs when the backbeat is aligns with beats two and four of a quadruple measure (that is, the expected timing of the backbeat).

13031.definition: A drum pattern in which the backbeat is twice as slow as usual (that is, the snare hits occur only on beat three of each measure, instead of beats two and four).

13034.definition: A drumbeat in which the kick drum plays on every beat, while the snare plays the last two parts of a tresillo rhythm.

13035.definition: A drumbeat in which the kick drum is sounded on every beat.

13036.definition: A kind of crash cymbal with an especially bright, forward, and splashy sound.

13037.definition: A meter with four beats, each of which divides into three. A time signature for compound quadruple will always have "12" as the top number. 12/8 is the most common compound quadruple meter.

13044.definition: A meter with three beats, each of which divides into three. The top number of a compound triple meter will always be "9". 9/8 is the most common compound triple meter.

13049.definition: A meter with two beats, each of which divides into three. The top number of a compound duple meter will always be "6". 6/8 is the most common compound duple meter, though 6/4 is also somewhat common.

13122.definition: A cylindrical drum, typically 14” in diameter, made of wood or metal with tensioned heads (or skins) on the top and bottom and a set of snare wires stretched below the bottom head to create the drum’s characteristic buzzing and cracking sounds. Played with force, it sounds like wood cracking or like a thunderclap. Played softly, it offers a range of effects from clicks and taps to buzzing rolls.

13123.definition: A large cylindrical drum, usually 18–24” in diameter, set on its side, typically with a wooden shell and two tensioned heads (the back one is sometimes removed or “ported,” meaning a circle is cut out), played with a foot pedal comprising a beater (a large mallet of felt, wood, or plastic) mounted to a cam and chain. The lowest-pitched drum in the kit, it is played with a foot pedal. It is originally based on a modified concert bass drum, and some still sound with the same booming quality. Other kick-drum sounds have a dull thud, or a sub-bass effect that (over the right speakers) is felt in the body as much as it is heard.

13124.definition: Drums of various sizes (diameters of 10–16” are most common), similar to the snare drum but with deeper bodies and lacking the snares. They have a more focused pitch fundamental than the snare and are higher-pitched than the kick. There are often three toms on a drum kit, with pitches that are low, middle, and high. The pitch can be a more or less prominent feature of the toms’ sound.

13125.definition: A large suspended cymbal, usually 20–24” in diameter. Depending on the thickness of the cymbal, the ride may sound like a warm wash of sound (thinner rides, common in jazz) or a sharp, high-pitched crunch (thicker rides, common in metal music). High, pure ringing sounds can be produced by playing the “bell” of the ride, located in the middle of the cymbal.

13126.definition: A pair of smaller cymbals, matched in size, typically 14” in diameter, mounted on a specially designed stand. The bottom cymbal sits upside down, unmoving, and the top cymbal is attached to the stand so that it can be controlled by a foot pedal. When struck, the hi-hats’ timbre depends on how open or closed the two cymbals are. The hi-hat is most often struck while closed, producing a characteristic, bright “tick tick tick”; the open sound has a more aggressive crashing or rattling quality; and a wide range of intermediate timbres are also available. When played with the foot pedal only, the cymbals make a splashing effect.

13130.definition: A mid-sized suspended cymbal. Can be various diameters (16–18” are typical) and thicknesses. Depending on size, contour, and playing technique, these can produce a variety of crashing, splashing, sizzling, and barking sounds.

13131.definition: Cymbals ranging in size (6–18” diameters are common) and thickness. Some have shapes and contours unlike other cymbals or are augmented with rivets or large holes. Depending on size, contour, and playing technique, these can produce a variety of crashing, splashing, sizzling, and barking sounds.

982.definition: A poetic foot consisting of one stressed syllable followed by one unstressed syllable.

983.definition: A poetic foot consisting of one stressed followed by one unstressed syllable.

1214.definition: Changing the direction of the motive (e.g. instead of going up, it goes down)

1934.definition: In the Classical-era of western, classical music—which spans the middle to the end of the 18th century—there were a specific set of standard cadence types that were used to close phrases. They were the perfect authentic cadence (PAC), the half cadence (HC), and the imperfect authentic cadence (IAC).

1936.term: Closed vs Open endings (a.k.a. sectional and continuous)
1936.definition: An important factor in influencing the stability of a section is how the section closes harmonically. If the section closes with an authentic cadence (either PAC or IAC) in the home key, the section is harmonically closed but any other close is considered harmonically open. Examples of open harmonic endings are half cadences and any type of cadence involving a modulation, that is, a PAC in the key of the dominant is still harmonically open because of the modulation.

1949.definition:
In the Classical-era of western, classical music—which spans the middle to the end of the 18th century—there were a specific set of standard modulation schemes that were used within a section of music. These are summarized below:

2174.definition: Sections that introduce, follow, or come between a work's core sections (A, B, primary & secondary themes, refrains, episodes, and developments/digressions/contrasting middles). Auxiliary sections are either external or internal. External Auxiliary Sections either introduce a piece/section (prefix) or follow the piece's/section's generic conclusion (suffix). Prefixes and suffixes come in small and large varieties. Internal auxiliary sections (connective sections) function to connect two core sections. Transitions generally help lead away from the piece's main section toward a contrasting section (B, secondary theme, episodes, developments/digressions/contrasting middles), and retransitions generally help to lead back to the piece's main section (usually A or a sonata form’s primary theme).

2534.definition: A method of specifying musical pitches by combining note names with octave designations

2541.definition: Pitches that are spelled the same but are one more more octaves apart

2547.definition: A series of eight notes (such as C to C)

2570.definition: A type of embellishing tone that holds a single pitch or pitch class in the bass while the chords change above it.

2849.definition: A seventh chord with a major triad and a major seventh.

2904.definition: A cadence that concludes with root position V to root position I, with the tonic in the soprano.

4060.definition: Having a different letter name but sounding the same (e.g. f-sharp and g-flat)

4237.definition: Modes are said to be parallel if they share a tonic pitch. For example, C major and C minor are parallel modes.

4753.definition: Establish a meter and tempo for musicians

5025.definition: Numbers that show the accentuation pattern of a hypermeter; they are placed above measures, centered

5366.definition: Shares a tonic with its parallel major

5369.definition: Shares a tonic with its parallel minor

5371.definition: Shares a key signature with its relative major

5372.definition: Shares a key signature with its relative minor

5377.definition: Accidentals (sharps or flats) in a certain combination that imply a particular note as tonic

5429.definition:
A root-position dominant will often take the form of any one of the following options and each provide an essentially equivalent overall harmonic effect:

V

V7

V64-53

V864-753

5556.definition: Scale-like patterns of half- and whole-steps

5702.definition: A "grid" of dots that represent beats and measures

6077.definition: A combination of size and quality to describe an interval

6092.definition: An interval a half-step larger than an augmented interval

6093.definition: An interval a half-step larger than a doubly augmented interval

6094.definition: An interval a half-step smaller than a diminished interval

6095.definition: An interval a half-step smaller than a doubly diminished interval

6164.definition: The same as modulation, a change of tonic.

6337.definition: The note of a triad or seventh chord a third above the root

6338.definition: The note of a triad or seventh chord a fifth above the root

7054.definition: Notes played or sung one at a time; also known as arpeggiating

8431.definition:
The distance from one pitch-class to another. Since pitch-classes are collections of all pitches related enharmonically and by octave equivalence, we need to define how to calculate this distance: 

if the ordering of pitch classes (pcs) matters, calculate the distance from pc 1 to pc2 in semitones as if you're going up to pc2, regardless of whether the actual pitch of pc 2 is higher or lower then pc1. Calculate the size within an octave.

If the order of the pcs doesn't matter, then just calculate the closest distance between the two pcs in semitones.

9428.definition: A system of naming chords that specifies the note name of the root, chord quality, and any alterations

10152.definition: two parts start an octave apart and both move in the same direction by the same interval to also end an octave apart.

10154.definition: two parts start an perfect fifth apart and both move in the same direction by the same interval to also end a perfect fifth apart

10155.definition: two parts begin any interval apart and move in the same direction to a perfect fifth or octave.

10222.definition: A larger set that contains some other set.

10655.definition: The meter written in the score may not be the meter that the listener perceives

11540.definition: A broad category of formal sections that introduce and repeat a work's primary musical ideas. Core sections are further divided into main core sections and contrasting core sections.

11844.definition: Similar motion into an octave. Also called a "hidden octave."

12366.definition: Tonerows with all eleven distinct intervals between neighboring pitches.
